title: Edit a Gene
principle: Cutting is the easy half. What the cell does next is the hard half.

t: Do the whole thing. Pick the target, aim, cut, check — and find out what you skipped.
Run a complete edit end to end. Every step you leave out fails in its own way, and one of the failures does not show up for years.
sub: The last check is the one people actually skip.
Not because it is difficult. Because nothing goes wrong immediately when you omit it.

t: Put each step in the job it does. Any part fits any slot, so the marking is on you.
Assign each component to its function. Placement is unconstrained; then five stress tests.

name: Know what you are aiming at
Target
fail: You have scissors and no idea where to point them.
Without a target sequence there is nothing to design a guide against.

name: Find it among three billion letters
Targeting
pass: The guide pairs with it and nothing else nearby.
fail: You know the address and have no way of getting there.
The nuclease has essentially no sequence preference of its own. Without a guide it is not a targeted tool at all.

name: Actually change something
Cutting
pass: A double-strand break, exactly where you meant.
fail: Targeting without a nuclease binds and does not edit — which is useful for other purposes, and is not an edit.

name: Get the change you wanted, not just a broken gene
Repair
pass: The cell repairs using your template.
Homology-directed repair installs the intended sequence.
fail: The cell repaired it badly and the gene is simply broken now.

Without a template the cell uses non-homologous end joining, which inserts or deletes a few bases at random. That disables a gene reliably — which is sometimes what you want, and is not the same as editing it.

name: Be sure nothing else got cut
Audit
pass: The intended edit is there, and nothing else changed.
Off-target screening across the genome confirms the edit is clean.
fail: A textbook edit, and you have no idea what else you cut.
This is the failure that does not announce itself. A cut in a tumour suppressor would not show for years, and the edit would look like a complete success in the meantime.

win: Aimed, cut, repaired the way you wanted, and checked. That is an edit.
All five hold, and the fifth is the one that separates a demonstration from a therapy.
lose: Read which test failed — it names what was in the wrong job.
Each failed trial names the step that was not performed. Reassign and re-test.

t: Cutting is the easy half. What the cell does next is the hard half.
CRISPR cuts. The cell repairs — and which repair pathway it uses determines whether you get the edit you designed or simply a broken gene.
Cas9 makes a double-strand break; the outcome depends on whether the cell uses non-homologous end joining, which disrupts, or homology-directed repair, which can install a chosen sequence.

HDR is far less efficient than end joining and works mainly in dividing cells, which is why precise correction remains much harder than disruption. It is also why base editing and prime editing were developed — they change letters without a double-strand break at all, and they are the more significant advance of the last few years.
sub: Breaking a gene is easy. Fixing one is not.
Reliable disruption and reliable correction are very different problems, and most early successes were disruptions.
The approved sickle-cell therapy is a disruption: it switches off a repressor so fetal haemoglobin comes back on.

That is worth noticing, because it is not what most people imagine gene therapy to be. Nothing was corrected — a different, already-present gene was un-silenced to compensate. Working out which achievable edit produces the wanted result is frequently more of the problem than the editing.

q: Why is the last check the one that matters most?
Why is off-target auditing the step most easily omitted?
Why does omitting the audit not look like a failure?
options: Skipping it looks exactly like success until years later
It is the most expensive step
why: If you cut somewhere you did not mean to, nothing goes wrong that day. The edit you wanted is there and it looks like it worked. The problem, if there is one, turns up years later.

Because its absence is invisible in the short run. Every other omission produces an immediate, obvious failure; this one produces a result indistinguishable from success until a consequence emerges much later.

It is the general shape of a safety check: the cases where it was needed are exactly the cases you would not otherwise detect, so the check appears to add nothing every time it comes back clean. That is why safety steps get dropped, and why the argument for keeping them has to be made on expected cost rather than on observed benefit.

t: The first approved CRISPR therapy edits cells outside the body, then puts them back.

Doing the editing in a dish means the result can be sequenced and checked before anything is returned to the patient — the audit step is performed while there is still a choice. Editing inside a living person removes that option, which is why it is a far harder approval problem and why the first approvals took the route they did.
